ceo_directive: Generate at least 5 design-around alternatives that achieve the same technical effect (CSF drainage + therapeutic retention) without reading on the A1 claim limitations L1..L6

limitations_frozen.L1: endovascular implant configured for CSF drainage
limitations_frozen.L2: size-selective filtration element within the shunt lumen
limitations_frozen.L3: filtration element permits passage of CSF fluid
limitations_frozen.L4: filtration element retains molecule above size threshold
limitations_frozen.L5: CSF drainage maintained during therapeutic retention
limitations_frozen.L6: integrated into eShunt anatomy (dural venous sinus deployment)

methodology.approach: Per-limitation avoidance: each design-around must NOT read on at least one limitation of L1..L6, AND must still achieve the therapeutic goal (CSF drainage + drug retention in subarachnoid space)
methodology.limitation_infringement_test: For each limitation, classify as READ_ON / DESIGN_AROUND / NOT_APPLICABLE based on whether the alternative would be literally or doctrine-of-equivalents covered.
methodology.obviousness_double_back_check: Each alternative must not be itself rendered obvious by a single reference (102-clean) or by a documented combination (103-clean)
methodology.engineering_feasibility: Each alternative must be technically implementable within the eShunt form factor

alternatives.name: Affinity-Bound Therapeutic Matrix
alternatives.core_concept: Replace size-selective membrane with a chemical affinity matrix lining the lumen. Drug-specific binding ligand (e.g., antibody fragment, aptamer, receptor mimic) is immobilized on the inner surface. CSF flows freely; therapeutic binds reversibly.

limitation_matrix.L2: DESIGN_AROUND (no size-selective filtration element — uses affinity binding instead)
limitation_matrix.L3: DESIGN_AROUND (no filtration element to pass CSF — open lumen)

alternatives.102_check: EnClear US12337140B2 discloses therapeutic inlet and pump but not affinity-bound matrix; 102-clean against known references.
alternatives.103_check: Combination of affinity matrices (known in dialysis columns) with CSF shunts (known) requires documented motivation; no obvious motivation in literature for combining the two for retention.
alternatives.engineering_feasibility: MEDIUM — surface chemistry must be CNS-biocompatible, binding capacity may saturate, regeneration in vivo challenging
alternatives.key_risk: Saturation of binding sites after chronic dosing; requires periodic flushing or desorption mechanism.
alternatives.potential_claim_set: CereVasc could file DA1 as a separate independent claim to block affinity-based competitors.

alternatives.name: Closed-Loop Active Pump Return
alternatives.core_concept: No membrane at all. An active bidirectional micropump withdraws CSF + drug from subarachnoid space, separates drug by centrifugal or charge-based microfluidic separation, returns drug to subarachnoid space while draining CSF to venous system.

limitation_matrix.L2: DESIGN_AROUND (no passive filtration element — active separation)
limitation_matrix.L3: DESIGN_AROUND (no filtration element, pump handles separation)
limitation_matrix.L4: DESIGN_AROUND (retention via active return, not size threshold)
limitation_matrix.L6: DESIGN_AROUND (mechanically more complex — may not fit eShunt form factor without redesign)

alternatives.102_check: Active CSF return pumps in implantable form are not directly disclosed in CereVasc or EnClear patents.
alternatives.103_check: Combination of implantable micropumps + microfluidic separation is known in insulin delivery; would need motivation to combine for CSF therapeutic return. Plausible 103 attack from insulin-pump + microfluidics prior art; must be analyzed.
alternatives.engineering_feasibility: LOW-MEDIUM — requires implanted power source, control electronics, microfluidic chip; chronic implantation in CNS adds risk
alternatives.key_risk: Battery life, electronic failure modes, biocompatibility of microfluidic chip surfaces
alternatives.potential_claim_set: CereVasc could file DA2 as a blocking claim on closed-loop active return.

alternatives.name: Magnetic Nanoparticle Retention
alternatives.core_concept: Drug is encapsulated in superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs). An external magnetic collar (worn externally) or an implanted magnetic ring at the dural venous sinus holds SPIONs in subarachnoid space while CSF drains. No intraluminal membrane.

limitation_matrix.L2: DESIGN_AROUND (no filtration element at all — magnetic field retains drug)
limitation_matrix.L4: DESIGN_AROUND (retention by magnetic force, not size threshold)
limitation_matrix.L6: DESIGN_AROUND (magnetic ring may sit at dural venous sinus but retention mechanism is external/field-based, not eShunt anatomy)

alternatives.102_check: Magnetic drug targeting patents exist (e.g., cancer therapy) but not specifically for CSF drainage + retention combination.
alternatives.103_check: Combining magnetic drug targeting (oncology) with CSF shunts — 103 motivation weaker; no known reference suggests this combination. Still requires explicit motivation analysis.
alternatives.engineering_feasibility: MEDIUM — SPIONs are clinically used (Feridex, Resovist); external magnetic collars feasible; chronic implantation of magnet ring at dural venous sinus is novel engineering
alternatives.key_risk: Magnetic field strength must be sufficient to retain nanoparticles against CSF outflow; SPION dose must be CNS-biocompatible; magnetic ring biocompatibility at venous sinus.
alternatives.potential_claim_set: CereVasc could file DA3 as blocking claim on magnetic retention of therapeutic in CSF shunt systems.

alternatives.name: Hydrogel Size-Exclusion Sleeve
alternatives.core_concept: Replace ePTFE membrane with a swellable hydrogel sleeve inside the lumen. Hydrogel mesh pore size depends on cross-linking density, not a porous membrane. Swelling creates dynamic exclusion barrier; CSF flows through mesh; drug (large) cannot.

limitation_matrix.L2: PARTIAL_DESIGN_AROUND — hydrogel is technically a 'filtration element' but it is not a 'size-selective' porous membrane in the ePTFE/track-etched sense; equivalency likely; L2 may still read on under doctrine of equivalents.
limitation_matrix.L4: READ_ON (retains large molecules by mesh exclusion)

alternatives.102_check: Hydrogels as filtration are known in dialysis literature.
alternatives.103_check: Hydrogel + CSF shunt combination is plausible; needs 103 motivation analysis.
alternatives.engineering_feasibility: MEDIUM-HIGH — hydrogels are biocompatible, can be tuned, but chronic swelling in vivo may degrade or occlude; fouling risk similar to ePTFE.
alternatives.key_risk: DOE risk on L2; hydrogel long-term stability in CSF is uncertain; may become the 'easier' design-around but also the easier design to design-around for competitors.
alternatives.potential_claim_set: Weaker independent claim — high DOE risk; consider as dependent claim only.

alternatives.name: Periodic Valve Interruption (Two-Phase Operation)
alternatives.core_concept: No membrane. Use a controllable one-way valve that alternates: closed phase (drug retained, no drainage) and open phase (CSF drains, drug partially lost but acceptable). Valve timing exploits CSF production rate vs drug diffusion rate.

limitation_matrix.L4: DESIGN_AROUND (no retention by size threshold — retention by valve closure)
limitation_matrix.L5: PARTIAL — CSF drainage is intermittent, not continuous; L5 says 'maintained during retention' which could be interpreted as continuous; risk of literal infringement.

alternatives.102_check: EnClear US12337140B2 discloses external CSF circuit with controller — but no endovascular valve timing for retention.
alternatives.103_check: Programmable shunt valves (Medtronic Strata, Codman Certas) are known; combining with timed drug-retention sequence requires explicit motivation. 103-clean against current literature.
alternatives.engineering_feasibility: HIGH — programmable valves are commercially available; only control algorithm is novel; integration is simplest of all alternatives.
alternatives.key_risk: Drug loss during 'open' phase; patient-specific CSF production rate varies; controller must adapt.
alternatives.potential_claim_set: CereVasc could file DA5 as a separate independent claim to block programmable-valve-timed retention competitors — this is the strongest design-around for blocking.

alternatives.name: Charge-Selective Ion-Exchange Barrier
alternatives.core_concept: Replace size-selective membrane with an ion-exchange membrane (anionic or cationic) that retains charged therapeutic molecules (e.g., charged peptides, oligonucleotides) while CSF (neutral) passes freely. Retention is by electrostatic repulsion, not size.

limitation_matrix.L2: DESIGN_AROUND — ion-exchange membrane is a 'selective' element but not 'size-selective'; may avoid L2 literal.

alternatives.102_check: Ion-exchange membranes are well-known in water treatment; not specifically applied to CSF shunts.
alternatives.103_check: Combining ion-exchange membrane with CSF shunt — motivation analysis required; plausible 103 attack from water-treatment + medical device prior art, but no specific reference located.
alternatives.engineering_feasibility: MEDIUM — ion-exchange membranes are thin, can be integrated; but chronic CSF exposure may foul or deplete charge; biocompatibility data limited for CNS-contact ion-exchange membranes.
alternatives.key_risk: Charge neutralization over time; fouling by charged CSF proteins; limited to charged therapeutics only (small neutral molecules cannot be retained).
alternatives.potential_claim_set: CereVasc could file DA6 to block charge-selective approaches — useful for oligonucleotide / peptide therapeutic classes.

alternatives.name: Osmotic Gradient Return (Semipermeable Membrane with Osmotic Return)
alternatives.core_concept: Semipermeable membrane allows CSF to drain to venous system but creates osmotic gradient that returns drug to subarachnoid space via osmotic pump mechanism. Drug is small enough to pass membrane but osmotic flow is engineered to return it.

limitation_matrix.L2: READ_ON (semipermeable membrane is a size-selective element)
limitation_matrix.L4: DESIGN_AROUND (drug passes membrane; retention is by osmotic return flow, not size threshold)

alternatives.102_check: Osmotic pumps are known (Durect DUROS); combining with CSF shunt novel.
alternatives.103_check: Plausible 103 attack from osmotic pump + CSF shunt literature; motivation analysis required.
alternatives.engineering_feasibility: LOW — osmotic gradients in CSF are delicate; chronic in vivo stability uncertain; osmolyte must be biocompatible.
alternatives.key_risk: Osmotic agent must be CNS-safe; mechanism is fragile to CSF composition changes.
alternatives.potential_claim_set: Weak — only L4 avoided; high DOE risk on L2/L4.

summary.rationale_for_strongest: Highest engineering feasibility, cleanest design-around of L2/L3/L4, simplest claim set to file, greatest commercial threat (existing programmable valve competitors could implement)
summary.rationale_for_weakest: Only avoids L4; high DOE risk on L2/L4; engineering feasibility low.
summary.rationale_for_companion_claims: Each covers a distinct non-size-selective retention mechanism. Filing these as dependent or independent claims creates a fence around the design-around space, blocking competitors from circumventing the A1 architecture.

design_around_gate_score.rationale: 7 alternatives generated (exceeds minimum 5). Strongest alternative (DA5) is engineering-feasible and patentability-clean. Weakest (DA7) is documented for completeness but not pursued. Each alternative includes 102/103 motivation analysis per protocol.
